esig.check_witness#22: This is a clock boundary: `v_act_at > clock_timestamp()` becomes `>=`. The two differ only when the stored act time equals, to the microsecond, the value clock_timestamp() returns inside this comparison. clock_timestamp() is the server wall clock read at evaluation. No caller or role can set or freeze it: search_path pins pg_catalog first, so it cannot be shadowed. The act time is fixed before the call. So no input, stored state or call sequence can produce the equal case deterministically. Any attempt is decided by microsecond timing, not by what the test controls. At the boundary the original accepts an act recorded exactly 'now', which is not in the future, and that is the correct reading.
esig.check_witness#2: The mutant turns `v_act is null OR jsonb_typeof(v_act) <> 'object' OR coalesce(v_act->>'device_id','')='' OR coalesce(v_act->>'at','')=''` into `(v_act is null AND jsonb_typeof(v_act) <> 'object') OR C OR D`, because AND binds tighter than OR. Whenever the first or the second term is true, v_act is SQL NULL or a non-object jsonb (null, string, number, boolean or array). For every one of those, the text-field operator `->> 'device_id'` returns NULL without raising, so term C, `coalesce(...,'') = ''`, is already true and ESIG-050 is still raised. When both terms are false, the change makes no difference. None of the terms has a side effect or can raise. The result is identical for every value of p_provided.
esig.check_witness#24: This is a clock boundary: `clock_timestamp() - v_act_at > v_window` becomes `>=`. The two differ only when the elapsed time equals the witness window (300 s by default) exactly to the microsecond, measured against the clock_timestamp() read inside the comparison. As for check_witness#22, that reading cannot be set, frozen or predicted by any input, state or call sequence, so the difference cannot be observed deterministically. At the boundary the original keeps the window inclusive: an act exactly one window old is 'within the witness window', which is correct.
esig.content_changed#10:
With the mutant (0220:309, `v_computed := true` becomes false) the hash `esig.content_hash_of(type, id, esig.provide(type, id))` is recomputed on every loop iteration instead of once per call. Results can differ only if that expression returns different values between two iterations of one call.
(1) content_hash_of is immutable over the provider output, and the provider contract in 0200 forbids a provider from changing data. A non-deterministic provider could never be signed: the hash at the challenge would differ from the hash at signing (EBMR-ESIG-012), so there would be no signature for the loop to visit.
(2) The only writes between iterations are the esig.signature_invalidation row (its stamp trigger and audit trigger) and the kernel.audit_business_event entry (a kernel.audit_event row, action BUSINESS or table esig.signature_invalidation). No trigger on those tables touches a signed table, and no registered provider's hashed fields (content, content_version) read them:
- esig_stub reads only esig.stub_signable.
- sample_record counts only audit events with table_name 'platform.stub_record' and action 'UPDATE'.
- The records and continuity providers have no signed tables. content_changed is owner-private (no grant; migration 0220 comment at line 489), so it runs only from esig.on_signed_content_change and never for those types.
(3) A concurrent commit cannot change hashed content between iterations. content_changed holds the aggregate's transaction-scoped advisory lock (esig.aggregate_lock) until commit, and every other change to that aggregate's hashed content goes through the same trigger, which waits on the same lock before its transaction can commit. For sample_record the changed row's row lock is also held. Only a superuser disabling triggers (session_replication_role = replica) could interleave a change; that is outside the trust boundary and is detected separately by esig.verify_signatures and the INV-09 invariant.
The only difference left is the number of provider calls, which is performance and not behaviour. Checked with a per-mutant run of all 7 new tests plus the group's existing tests: none detects it.
